name: Pearl extract

lead: Pearl extract is made from ground pearls or nacre and is used in traditional Chinese medicine and in brightening and anti-aging skin care. Its use is documented for well over a thousand years.
Research is mostly in cells and animals, with a few papers on lightening and melasma. Controlled human trials for appearance are limited.

paras: Laboratory papers propose antioxidant effects, support for fibroblast migration and, in one report, antagonism of endothelin as a route to skin lightening.

Sources describe it as widely used topically; Wikipedia notes oral doses in traditional medicine and that excessive amounts may cause calcium toxicity. Little safety data from controlled skin trials was found.

trials.title: Study of the Impact of Mother-of-pearl Nutritional Supplementation on the Prevention of Post-menopausal Osteoporosis

lead: Pearl extract and pearl powder are preparations made from pearls or nacre, used in traditional Chinese medicine and in cosmetics marketed for brightening and anti-aging.[1][2] Pearl medicine in China has a history of more than 2,000 years, and it is described as used to calm the mind, clear the eyes and soothe skin.[3]

Published research on pearl extract in skin applications consists largely of laboratory and animal studies, such as work on fibroblast migration, UV-exposed skin cells and photoaging in mice, along with a small number of reports on skin lightening and melasma.[4][5][6][7][8] Evidence from controlled human trials for appearance outcomes is limited.
infobox: Ground pearls or nacre, often freshwater pearls[1]

paras: Pearl powder is made by sterilising freshwater or low-grade saltwater pearls and milling them finely; it is sold as a powder or mixed into creams.[1] It is described as containing amino acids, trace minerals and a high concentration of calcium.[1] Pearl powder is distinguished from nacre powder, which comes from the inner layer of the shell.[3] Reviews describe extraction of matrix proteins from both as a route to cosmetic and medical ingredients.[3]

Use in China is documented from at least 320 AD, and the Ming-era Bencao Gangmu is said to credit pearl powder with stimulating skin growth and reducing sun damage; Empress Wu Zetian reportedly used it.[1] It was also used in Ayurveda, and in medieval and early modern Europe for several conditions; in the 19th century it was used as a skin whitener, though one period source condemned it as harmful.[1]

Pearl extract is marketed for brightening and as an anti-aging ingredient, and is a common component of Asian skin-care products.[1] Proponents cite its traditional reputation and ingredient content; researchers describe antioxidant, anti-aging and tonic activities in laboratory settings.[2]

A paper titled "Soluble Pearl Extract provides effective skin lightening by antagonizing endothelin" reports on a proposed mechanism for lightening,[5] and a 2025 paper reports that pearl extract alleviates melasma by targeting CREB1.[7] A 2022 study examined a pearl extract from Pinctada fucata martensii in UV-induced photoaging in mice.[6]

Few clinical studies on appearance outcomes were found. Most work is laboratory or animal research: pearl extract enhanced fibroblast migration in a wound-healing model,[2] a pearl extract gel was reported to have anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects on UVB-irradiated skin cells,[4] and a rat study examined pearl and premature ovarian failure.[9] A registered trial (NCT05571514, recruiting, n=200) is testing mother-of-pearl supplements for postmenopausal osteoporosis, not appearance.[10]
